lines.say: Four sealed boxes, one hides a prize. Can we find it in one look?
A helper knows which, and won't tell, but will quietly mark it.
Grover search can, and it's like pushing a swing: each push lifts it higher.
Each box gets an amplitude, a number whose square is its chance of showing up.
Two qubits, quantum bits, name the boxes; an H gate on each spreads them evenly.
Every box gets amplitude one half: a one in four chance.
Now the helper, the oracle, flips the sign of the prize's amplitude to minus one half.
Squared, that's still a quarter, so the odds haven't changed.
Next, the diffuser reflects every amplitude around their average, now one quarter.
The other three sit a quarter above it, so they land a quarter below, at zero.
The prize sits three quarters below, so it's flung three quarters above, to one.
That's interference: amplitudes combine, the prize grows, the rest cancel, and one look always finds it.
With sixteen boxes, we repeat both steps, one push per round.
For N boxes, the sweet spot is about pi over four root N rounds, three here. Push longer and it swings back.
But a real swing gains energy, and this never does: the chances always add to one.
The prize only grows because every other box shrinks.
It never opens every box at once. It reshapes amplitudes so one look is likely right.
So mark the answer with a sign, reflect around the average, and repeat about pi over four root N times.
